hysterical

/hi-STER-i-kul/ — stress on STER · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Someone who is hysterical is overwhelmed by extreme emotion, especially fear or distress, and loses control of their reactions.

Callers grew hysterical as the flood sirens kept sounding.

Worked Example

When the power went out during the thunderstorm, some passengers on the train became hysterical, banging on windows and shouting uncontrollably.

Hysteria (uncontrollable emotion) + -al = characteristic of hysteria. The passengers were overwhelmed by fear and losing emotional control—exactly what hysterical means. They weren't just scared; they were experiencing hysteria.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

panicked: Panicked means seized by sudden, overwhelming fear — the jolt when smoke fills a room. Hysterical is about what happens to control: emotion so extreme that reactions run wild, whether the trigger was sudden or slow. Panic names the fear's arrival; hysterical names the collapse of composure.

distraught: Distraught means so upset that clear thinking is gone — an inner state of churning grief or worry. Hysterical points at the outside: sobbing, shouting, shaking that cannot be reined in. A distraught parent may sit silent and hollow; a hysterical one cannot stop the outburst.

overwrought: Overwrought means strained past calm — nerves wound so tight that a person is tense, teary, and ready to snap. Hysterical is the snap itself: control of one's reactions is already gone. An overwrought witness is barely holding together; a hysterical one has stopped holding together at all.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

calm: free of strong emotion or agitation

composed: keeping self-control under pressure

Where it sits · how completely emotional control is lost — nervous → agitated → frantic → hysterical

nervous vs. hysterical: A nervous person feels jittery inside, but a hysterical person has completely lost control of their emotions.

agitated vs. hysterical: Someone agitated is visibly worked up, while someone hysterical is so overwhelmed they can no longer calm themselves at all.

frantic vs. hysterical: Frantic means wild with worry but still functioning, whereas hysterical means runaway emotion has taken over entirely.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — hysteric

Root — hysteric: affected by hysteria — runaway, uncontrollable emotion (Greek (via Latin))

Suffix — -al

Suffix — -al: characteristic of; relating to (Latin (-alis))

Put it together

Put it together: Hysteria names runaway, uncontrollable emotion, and -al means 'characteristic of.' So hysterical describes someone characteristic of that runaway state — overwhelmed by extreme fear or excitement and unable to keep self-control.

Use the root in a new word: hysteria

Word Building

Word Choice

formal-to-colloquial

Use hysterical to describe someone who has lost emotional control due to overwhelming fear, grief, or distress — not just strong feelings, but a breakdown of composure. Be aware: in informal speech, people sometimes stretch 'hysterical' to mean just 'very funny,' but the precise sense is 'emotionally overwhelmed.'
